title: Comparing the complexity of wayfinding tasks in built environments
central_proposition: A computational method using a choice-clue wayfinding model, derived from image schemata extracted from natural language, can effectively compare the complexity of wayfinding tasks in built environments, enabling the identification of architectural problems prior to construction.

concept_definitions.name: Wayfinding
concept_definitions.definition: Based on 'a consistent use and organization of definite sensory cues from the external environment'.

concept_definitions.name: Image Schemata
concept_definitions.definition: Recurring imaginative patterns that people use to comprehend and structure their experiences while moving through and interacting with their environment.

concept_definitions.name: Choice-Clue Wayfinding Model
concept_definitions.definition: A simple wayfinding model that considers two critical elements: choices and clues to measure wayfinding task complexity.

concept_definitions.name: Choices
concept_definitions.definition: Relate directly to decision points in wayfinding, representing the opportunity to select among different paths.

concept_definitions.name: Enforced Decision Points
concept_definitions.definition: Points where subjects have one obvious choice to continue the wayfinding task (choice = 1).

concept_definitions.name: Decision Points
concept_definitions.definition: Points where subjects have more than one choice to continue the wayfinding task (choices > 1).

concept_definitions.name: Clues
concept_definitions.definition: Properties of the built environment, such as signs and architectural features, that people use to make wayfinding decisions.

concept_definitions.name: Good Clues
concept_definitions.definition: Complete clues that enable people to decide about the correct continuation of their path.

concept_definitions.name: Poor Clues
concept_definitions.definition: Incomplete or misleading clues that do not enable people to decide about the correct continuation of their path.

concept_definitions.name: Environmental Communication
concept_definitions.definition: Transfer of orientation, wayfinding (direction), and other information within the built environment by means of signs and other communications devices or architectural features to enable people to reach destinations.

concept_definitions.name: Imageability
concept_definitions.definition: That quality in a physical object which gives it a high probability of evoking a strong image in any given observer.

concept_definitions.name: Landmark Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Comprises salient points of reference in the environment.

concept_definitions.name: Route Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Puts landmarks into a sequence (e.g., navigation paths).

concept_definitions.name: Survey or Configurational Knowledge
concept_definitions.definition: Allows people to locate landmarks and routes within a general frame of reference (i.e., incorporating Euclidean measurements).

argument_structure: The paper first reviews existing wayfinding research, highlighting the gap in computational models that neglect the process of structuring tasks and space. It then proposes a novel choice-clue wayfinding model and details how image schemata, extracted from natural language, can operationalize its critical elements (choices and clues). This method is then applied in a comparative case study of two airports to demonstrate its applicability and validate its ability to differentiate wayfinding complexity.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: People structure their spatial experiences using recurring mental patterns called image schemata. These schemata, particularly PATH and LINK, can be identified from natural language descriptions of wayfinding. The number of distinct PATH schemata at a viewpoint determines the 'choices' (decision point vs. enforced decision point), while the presence and quality of LINK schemata (and their relation to PATH) determine the 'clues' (good, poor, no clues). Combinations of choices and clues define six situations, with 'decision points with poor/no clues' representing problem areas. A higher count of viewpoints falling into these problem areas indicates greater wayfinding complexity, as these situations increase cognitive load, uncertainty, and the likelihood of errors or getting lost.

findings.consequent: Cognitive map development and representational accuracy
findings.mechanism: Environmental complexity makes it harder for people to construct and develop accurate mental representations of space.
findings.quote: Complex environmental structures can lead to slower development of cognitive maps and also to representational inaccuracies.

findings.mechanism: Visual access allows subjects to perceive more of the environment, aiding orientation, especially when sight is restricted.
findings.quote: visual access as an important factor, because wayfinding performance of subjects with restricted sight improved less over time.

findings.mechanism: Floor plans provide external spatial information that compensates for limited visual perception, aiding orientation.
findings.quote: The performance of subjects with restricted sight using floor plans improved as fast as that of subjects with no restricted sight; floor plans therefore counteract the negative effect.

findings.mechanism: Complex spatial layouts increase cognitive load and make it harder to form cognitive maps, leading to poorer wayfinding.
findings.quote: an increase in floor-plan complexity leads to a decrease in wayfinding performance.

findings.mechanism: Signs provide explicit directional and identification information, guiding wayfinding decisions.
findings.quote: The presence of signage was an important factor but could not compensate for floor-plan complexity.

findings.antecedent: Spatial structure of the physical environment
findings.mechanism: The inherent organization and layout of the environment directly shape how people navigate and make decisions.
findings.quote: the spatial structure of the physical environment has a strong influence on people's wayfinding behavior.

findings.mechanism: Direct visual access reduces uncertainty and provides clear perceptual cues for navigation.
findings.quote: For passengers arriving at the gate with direct visual access to the baggage claim, wayfinding was easier.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with the environment (frequency of prior use)
findings.mechanism: Prior experience builds stronger cognitive maps and reduces the need for active information processing, making navigation more efficient.
findings.quote: people's familiarity with the environment also has a big impact on wayfinding performance: frequency of prior use had a big facilitating effect.

findings.antecedent: Fewer decision points on a route
findings.mechanism: Fewer choices reduce cognitive load and the potential for errors, simplifying the navigation task.
findings.quote: fewer decision points on any route and redundancy in wayfinding information are also facilitating effects.

findings.mechanism: Multiple cues confirming the correct path reduce uncertainty and increase confidence in decisions.
findings.quote: fewer decision points on any route and redundancy in wayfinding information are also facilitating effects.

findings.consequent: Difficulty of performing a wayfinding task
findings.mechanism: Each decision point requires cognitive effort to evaluate options and select a path, increasing overall task difficulty.
findings.quote: The number of decision points directly influences the difficulty of performing a wayfinding task (Arthur and Passini, 1992).

findings.antecedent: Viewpoint with Choices > 1 AND poor clue(s)
findings.mechanism: Multiple options combined with incomplete or misleading information make it difficult to select the correct path, leading to errors or frustration.
findings.quote: Decision points with incomplete or misleading clues pose wayfinding problems for people.

findings.antecedent: Viewpoint with Choices > 1 AND no clue(s)
findings.mechanism: Without any information to guide decisions among multiple options, people are unable to determine the correct path, leading to them getting lost.
findings.quote: Decision points without any clues form the worst scenario for wayfinding. At such points people are lost.

findings.antecedent: Viewpoint with Choice = 1 AND poor clue(s) OR no clue(s)
findings.mechanism: Even with only one path, a lack of confirming or reliable clues prevents people from being confident in their direction, leading to uncertainty and hesitation.
findings.quote: Even though there is only one way to proceed, people might hesitate to follow it because poor clues do not reassure them that they are still on the right track.

findings.antecedent: Viewpoint with Choice = 1 AND good clue(s)
findings.mechanism: A single obvious path combined with clear, confirming information makes navigation straightforward and confident.
findings.quote: At an enforced decision point, people are forced to continue in one direction. Good clues confirm that people are on the right track. Therefore, wayfinding is easy at these points.

findings.antecedent: Viewpoint with Choices > 1 AND good clue(s)
findings.mechanism: Multiple options are easily navigated when complete, easy-to-read, and understandable clues clearly indicate the correct path.
findings.quote: At decision points people need good clues to choose the correct path. If clues are complete, easy to read, and easy to understand, wayfinding at those points is easy.

findings.antecedent: Frankfurt International Airport wayfinding task (departure hall to gate)
findings.mechanism: The analysis using the choice-clue model showed a higher rating of points within 'problem areas' for Frankfurt (2) compared to Vienna (1).
findings.quote: The wayfinding task 'going from the departure hall to the gate' has a higher rating of points within 'problem areas' at Frankfurt International (2) than at Vienna International (1).

findings.mechanism: Architectural layout and signage create more points where passengers must choose between multiple paths.
findings.quote: Frankfurt has more decision points (10) than Vienna (5).

findings.mechanism: Signage and architectural features are less effective or misleading, providing incomplete information for wayfinding decisions.
findings.quote: The sum of all 'poor' clues totals 14 in Frankfurt and only 5 in Vienna.

findings.mechanism: Lack of adequate signage or architectural features means no information is available to guide wayfinding decisions at critical points.
findings.quote: The sum of all missing clues totals 7 in Frankfurt and only 3 in Vienna.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Environments with a higher count of viewpoints classified as 'problem areas' by the choice-clue model (i.e., Choices > 1 with poor or no clues) will result in higher perceived wayfinding complexity and more wayfinding errors.
The proposed choice-clue model, operationalized through image schemata extracted from natural language, can predict the relative complexity of wayfinding tasks in different built environments.
bridge_warrants: The method aligns with Naive Geography by developing formal models of geographic space that match human cognition.
Clues in the model relate directly to Norman's (1988) concept of 'knowledge in the world'.
The approach explores 'practical space' as defined by Piaget and Inhelder (1967).
The model's concepts are based on observations by Lynch (1960) regarding spatial elements like paths and landmarks.
methodological_critiques: Most existing computational wayfinding models focus on knowledge representation (e.g., cognitive maps) and do not consider the process of how people structure wayfinding tasks and space.
Previous wayfinding research often concentrated on the description of the cognitive map, neglecting affective and logistical concerns.
Signage alone is often insufficient to overcome architectural failures in facilitating wayfinding.
model_structure: The choice-clue wayfinding model is a 2x3 matrix (Figure 1) that categorizes viewpoints in a wayfinding task based on two critical elements: 'choices' (Choice = 1 for enforced decision points, Choices > 1 for decision points) and 'clues' (good, poor, or no clues). This matrix defines six situations, each representing a different level of wayfinding complexity. Complexity is measured by counting the number of viewpoints that fall into 'problem areas' (situations with Choices > 1 combined with poor or no clues).
limitations: The demonstration of the method is based on a small number of interviews, requiring a more sophisticated and extended experimental design to verify cross-cultural universality of image-schematic representations.
The study used slides to simulate environments rather than real-world application space, which may limit ecological validity.
Further research is needed to establish which specific image schemata are most relevant for comparing wayfinding tasks in built environments.
Image schemata often occur in tightly coupled blocks, and more research is needed on how these blocks are structured and connected.
A more comprehensive set of image schemata needs to be formalized in an integrated algebra for robust representation and simulation in spatial information and design systems.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Wayfinding is a basic activity that people do throughout their lives as they navigate from one place to another. Many theories of spatial cognition have been developed to account for this behavior. However, most of the computational models focus on knowledge representation (for example, cognitive maps) and do not consider the process of how people structure wayfinding tasks and space. In this paper we present a computational method to compare the complexity of wayfinding tasks in built environments. As a measure for such complexity, we use a simple wayfinding model that consists of two critical elements: choices and clues. We show that elements of people's perception and cognition can be used to determine the elements of the wayfinding model and, therefore, to compare the complexity of wayfinding tasks in built environments. A case study of wayfinding in airports demonstrates the applicability of the method. The integration of this method into the computational design process of built environments will help to identify architectural problems with regard to wayfinding prior to construction.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that environmental complexity impacts wayfinding performance and cognitive map development by influencing cognitive load and the efficiency of spatial information processing.

steps.from_construct: Increased environmental complexity (e.g., numerous decision points, visual ambiguity, lack of distinct landmarks)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Individuals form internal cognitive representations (cognitive maps) of their environment to facilitate navigation and spatial understanding.
A conceptual framework for systematically comparing and analyzing the complexity of wayfinding tasks in built environments, considering both structural and informational characteristics.
